title: Diwali Meets Chuseok in Delhi as K-Pop Band NTX Headlines Korea Culture Day
excerpt: Korean Cultural Centre India's two-day festival at Select CITYWALK paired Diwali with Korea's Chuseok harvest festival, with six performance teams and NTX singing 'Kesariya' for a Delhi audience.
body:
• Korean Cultural Centre India held Korea Culture Day 2026 at Select CITYWALK in New Delhi on October 23, running into October 24, under the theme "One Light, Two Cities."
  • The festival paired India's Diwali with Korea's Chuseok harvest festival, with organisers and South Korea's ambassador stressing their shared focus on family, community and light.
  • Six Korean performance teams took the stage, from Taekwondo and traditional music to K-pop boy band NTX, who sang "Kesariya" and danced to "Kaala Chashma" and "Koi Mil Gaya."
  • For diaspora readers, the event is a reminder that India-Korea cultural exchange is expanding beyond K-dramas and K-pop into food, games and city-level festivals — with more programmes promised in major Indian cities.

One light, two festivals

Diwali met Chuseok in New Delhi this week as Korean Cultural Centre India staged Korea Culture Day 2026 at Select CITYWALK on October 23. The two-day festival, held under the theme "One Light, Two Cities," folded the centre's annual Rang De Korea festival into a broader Korea Culture Day and drew a direct parallel between India's festival of lights and Korea's autumn harvest festival.

Speaking at the opening ceremony, South Korea's Ambassador to India, Lee Seong-ho, said that despite their distinct traditions, Diwali and Chuseok share a common spirit of cherishing family and community and sharing light with one another. He argued that cultural exchange goes beyond presenting one country's culture to another, serving instead as a way to build mutual understanding, foster new connections and deepen friendship between India and Korea, according to coverage of the event.

K-Pop takes centre stage

Six performance teams from Korea showed the range of the country's performing arts across the two days. The Daekyeung University Taekwondo Demonstration Team opened with a choreographed display of Korea's martial art. Eolssigu presented music rooted in Korean traditional heritage, violin duo Ayuni added a classical crossover set, vocal quartet Atti Classic performed vocal crossover, and DEEPER blended electronic dance music with live instruments.

The headline act was K-pop boy band NTX, who closed the programme and crossed over to the home audience: the group sang "Kesariya" from the Hindi film Brahmastra and danced to a medley of Indian songs including "Kaala Chashma" and "Koi Mil Gaya," The World Times reported. Beyond the stage, visitors sampled Korean food, traditional games and K-content, with participating brands including Star Entertainment, the Indian distributor of the film Hope, alongside Orion and MIXXO of E-Land. A corridor-of-light installation formed the visual centrepiece, built around the festival's theme.

"This event has been designed to give a diverse range of visitors, including young people in India, the opportunity to experience Korean culture firsthand and deepen mutual understanding between the two countries."

— Kang Kwon Su, Director, Korean Cultural Centre India

Why the pairing matters

The timing was deliberate. At their summit in April 2026, the leaders of India and South Korea agreed to expand cultural and people-to-people exchanges alongside economic and strategic cooperation, with an emphasis on fostering greater understanding of each other's cultures and traditions. Korea Culture Day is the public-facing side of that commitment: a free, mall-based festival designed to reach young Indians where they already are, rather than inside a diplomatic compound.

The Diwali-Chuseok pairing does specific work in that effort. Both festivals gather families, give thanks and centre on light and renewal, which lets organisers present Korean culture as familiar rather than foreign. For Indian audiences whose entry point has been K-pop and Korean dramas, the programme deliberately pushed further — into traditional music, martial arts, food and games — to widen what "Korean culture" means in India.

What comes next

Kang Kwon Su, Director of Korean Cultural Centre India, said the centre will continue to expand cultural exchange programmes in major Indian cities, creating more opportunities for local and Korean cultures to come together. For diaspora families and for Indians with Korean business, study or travel ties, that means more of these festivals are likely to appear outside Delhi as well. Readers who missed the Delhi edition can watch for the centre's next city programmes, where the same mix of performance, food and hands-on cultural experiences is expected to return.
